Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00767

Insofar as these bodies exist, they share in knowledge, power, and life. But their parts are spread through space and matter. Their parts are far apart in time. They mix with absence and darkness, so they are unaware of themselves and forget their own nature. They are submerged in matter, scattered across the physical world. They cannot remember their original home of light and wholeness. Even so, their weak existence and small share of light come from existence itself. Through God's care and continued gift, they can receive some life and light. This frees them, in part, from the rule of absence and darkness, so they do not fall into complete nonexistence.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00768

The first covering of form given to them by eternal mercy keeps them from scattering and flowing apart. Next comes the form that holds their parts together against forces that would break them apart. Then they receive what they need from outside to strengthen them and replace what they lose. Growth adds size and completes each individual. The power of reproduction then continues their existence through similar beings. After giving them these forms, God's care guides them toward closeness and union, as their capacities grow little by little, until they return to the world of the afterlife and the level of the intellect they have gained. This is one basic principle.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00769

Remember, too, that all bodies can receive a nobler life and a higher form of completion than the one already within them. What prevents some of them is their low position in the world of separation and opposition. Each is bound to a single, divided identity that conflicts with others and harms them, just as they harm it. When this force of division and conflict weakens, matter becomes ready for a higher form: one that is less divided and more united.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00770

The elements are so low, divided, and far from unity—and their qualities and forms clash so strongly—that they resist the life of the soul and intellect. But when their opposed qualities weaken and their own existence grows firmer, this conflict fades. Then they can receive another kind of existence and a higher form. With greater balance, they stand between all the elements: in one way they are free of them; in another, they hold them together in a finer unity. As they move further from the opposed extremes, they become ready for a higher life and a more complete form. Step by step, they rise until their form becomes that of a soul joined to the Active Intellect, a light from God, a noble image of Him, a complete word, and a greatest name. This is another basic principle.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00771

Keep in mind that every complete form contains all the lower forms within it, but in a finer, nobler, and simpler way. An incomplete form can exist only through another form that completes it, surrounds it, preserves it, and brings it from possibility to reality and from lack to fullness. Without the complete form, the incomplete one would not exist. A lower thing cannot stand by itself; it depends on what is fuller. Possibility depends on what is actual, and what is actual on what must be. Completion comes before incompletion, what must be before what may be, existence before nonexistence, what is actual before what is only possible, and a defined form before something still undefined.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00772

People are misled because in this world they see what is incomplete come first in time: a seed before a fruit, or a fetus before an animal. But what comes first in time is not the true cause of what comes later. It only prepares the material for it. Those earlier states of absence, power, and possibility must themselves depend on a real form that exists and gives them their place.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00773

Once we understand these principles, we can see that every elemental and lifeless form must have another, more complete form closely joined to it, present within it though hidden from our senses. This form is not the Active Intellect acting directly, as followers of Aristotle say, nor is it one of the separate intellects that rule the kinds of things, acting without any intermediate link, as the Illuminationists say. As we explained, a higher cause can act on a lower thing only through something suited to both. Otherwise, another link would be needed between each pair, without end. So there must be a real inner connection between what gives a thing its form and what receives that form.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00774

Every natural form therefore has an unseen form: this is the next life's image of it, just as its own image is the first life's form. The next life has ranks, just like this one, from higher to lower. In the afterlife, each creature is returned to a place that matches its rank here: the nobler to the nobler, the lower to the lower. If a form changes here from a lower state to a higher one, as a lifeless thing becomes a plant or a plant becomes an animal, it returns in the next life according to the form it has reached. It is like a person who leaves disbelief for faith, or gives up wrongdoing and repents: their return changes from one level of Hell to a level of paradise, according to their state in this life.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00775

Every natural thing therefore has a soul-form in the next life, and that soul-form has an intellectual form in a world above it. Each higher world has many ranks. Its highest level joins with the lowest level of the world above it. A form in the lower world is like matter for the form above it. As we have seen, matter and form are joined; the form completes the matter and is its return and final home. Sense forms, when made finer, become matter for soul-forms, which in turn become matter for intellectual forms. Sense depends on the soul; the soul on intellect; and intellect on the Creator.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00776

The greatest philosopher says that the matter of intellect is noble because it is simple and intellectual, but intellect is even more complete and contains it. The matter of soul is noble because it is simple and belongs to the soul, but soul is more complete and contains it. With the help of intellect, the soul gives it wonderful effects. The soul is nobler than its matter because it surrounds it and shapes it into wonderful images. We can see this in the world of the senses. Anyone who looks at it is amazed, especially by its size, beauty, nobility, constant movement, and the spirits that live within it: animals, air, plants, and all other things.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00777

When you see the things we can sense in this lower world, use your reason to look toward the higher, true world, of which this one is only an image. There you will see the same things as lasting, intellectual realities, filled with virtues and pure life, untouched by impurity. They are full of knowledge and wisdom because light flows over them. Each seeks to rise toward the rank of the next and draw nearer to the first light that shines on that world. That world contains all lasting things that do not die, and includes all intellects and souls. This account clearly supports what we are saying.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00778

Another proof that natural forms have soul-forms, which are their inner reality and return, and intellectual forms above those, is found in our own perception. When we sense something outside us, its form appears in our senses in a way different from its outward form. Our senses belong to the animal level, which has sense perception but nothing higher. When the form enters a sense and completes it, another, finer, and nobler form arises from it. Our power of imagination takes on this new form. We have proved that imagination and the forms held in it are free of matter. From the form in imagination, yet another form enters our intellect. If each thing we sense had no inner connection to its image in imagination and its form in intellect, this progression could not happen.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00779

The same is true in the opposite direction. When we understand an intellectual form, a matching image appears in imagination. When the image becomes strong, it affects our senses, and a form appears before them, as in the verse: “Then she saw him as a well-formed man.” This is how the Prophet saw Gabriel and the angels in this world.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00780

These proofs show that every natural form in the visible world has a soul-form in the unseen world. That form is its return and final home after its material support disappears. It is already joined to the natural form and sustains it. But because the natural form is buried in darkness and absence, and submerged in matter and bodies, only people of knowledge and insight can clearly see its return to the soul-form that gives it life.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00781

When natural forms fall apart as their material support decays, they leave their bodily coverings and appear in that world of knowledge, insight, and certainty. They are gathered there, as the Qur'an says, “Hell will be brought into view for all to see,” and, “No indeed! They will soon know. Again, no indeed! They will soon know. No indeed! If only you knew with certainty, you would see Hell.” The image of Hell that people will see in the next life is the inner reality of this lower world. Here, its fire burns bodies and changes their skin. There, it appears with its chains, shackles, scorpions, and snakes. Its pleasures and desires appear as fires that burn the heart and torment the soul. Its food and drink appear as the tree of zaqqum and boiling water, which increase the soul's hunger and thirst, heat and pain.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00782

The sixth claim: what happens to matter and material bodies, and the end of evil people and demons. We have shown that all beings with a real form naturally seek their ends and the completion that leads them to higher ends, until they reach the one end with nothing beyond it. But some things exist only as possibilities or preparations for other things, which are their forms and completions. These include matter, motion, power, and time.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00783

The same is true of bodily extension, which can be divided and broken apart and naturally tends to fade and flow away. If souls and natural powers did not hold it together and give it unity, its parts would separate from one another. Each part would be absent from the others; the presence of one would mean that another was away. What has no unity in itself has no existence. Time too is nothing but passing and running out.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00784

So the end of these things is decay and disappearance. They cannot pass from this world, which is a source of evils, darkness, and absence, into the lasting world of life. If they did, what cannot remain would become lasting, nonexistence would become existence, change would become permanence, and death would become life. Thus matter, motion, and time, and the body considered only as something that changes and decays, return to nonexistence.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00785

The same applies to things in the soul. Cowardice, ignorance, dullness, and similar qualities end in destruction if they are simple and not mixed with active evil. If they are mixed with defiance, pride, or hypocrisy, they end in severe suffering and painful punishment. As we explained in our discussion of cause and effect, people can be drawn toward false ends. These begin with confused ideas, empty hopes, and harmful desires. Each kind of corrupt desire has its own tyrant that leads a person toward a limited goal in this world. But those limited goals and imagined purposes are corrupt and short-lived. Anyone ruled by such a tyrant, misled by desire and following it, is ruled by things that belong to this passing life. As this world fades, its tyrant and followers also fade. They move further into nonexistence and fall through lower states until they reach the home of ruin, the final resting place of those who do evil.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00786

A final word in support of our argument. We have shown that God's power never stops giving existence to what lies below it. His power has no limit in strength, duration, or number. First, He gives existence to intellect and forms it in His image, before giving existence to anything else. His care does not allow a lower being to appear before a higher one. The higher comes first, then the next higher, step by step, until the lowest possible level is reached.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00787

So the Creator first brought the First Intellect into existence, complete and perfect. But the intellect too is complete after the First, with no limit in how long or how many it can bring forth, though not in the strength of each one. It cannot stop at itself and produce nothing else. So it gives its light and power to the soul, as far as a giver and receiver can be close to one another.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00788

When the soul is filled with light, power, virtue, and goodness, it too cannot stop at itself. These qualities it receives from intellect make it long to resemble and join with intellect. So it gives its light and virtues to what lies below it, but through change over time. If its existence were already complete, it would be intellect, not soul. Its light and beauty fill this world through the forms of kinds and the natures of bodies: spheres, stars, animals, plants, minerals, and elements.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00789

Those forms too are made by nature to give to what lies below them and act upon it, following God's law and the pattern He has set. But material nature is the lowest of all forms. It can produce nothing beyond matter, which gives things only the ability to exist, and motion, which brings what is possible into being. Matter and motion therefore bring things into being, then allow them to pass away. They begin and end; they appear and disappear. This world must one day be ruined, and everything on earth must pass away, as God says: “Everyone on it will pass away, but the face of your Lord will remain, full of majesty and honor.” Nature then returns to soul, soul to intellect, and intellect to God, the One who rules over all. God asks, “Whose is the kingdom today?” and answers, “It is God's, the One, the All-Powerful.” He also says, “The Trumpet will be blown, and all who are in the heavens and on earth will fall senseless, except those God wills. Then it will be blown again, and they will rise and look around.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00790

When these things return to their original homes, leaving behind the world of motion, change, evil, pain, and bodily death—and when souls leave behind fear and collapse—God's mercy will give them life again, a life without death, and an existence that will not end. God says, “Then it will be blown again, and they will rise and look around,” and, “The earth will shine with the light of its Lord.” That earth of the next life is a soul-form, alive and ready to receive the light of intellect that flows from God. It may also mean this earth after God takes it into His hand, when it becomes a soul-form that can be drawn into God's care, as He says, “The whole earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection.” To take something into one's hand means it remains present but is raised to a nobler form, as food becomes part of the one who eats it. To fold something up, by contrast, means it no longer has its own separate existence. So God's taking the earth into His hand means that its natural form changes into a soul-form of the next life, as the verse says, “On the day the earth is changed into another earth.” Folding the heavens means they lose their separate selves and unite with intellect, which is God's right hand. Pure intellect loses itself and remains through God.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00791

Everything in the next life exists as an image perceived by the soul. It does not need a material subject or base, which has no life of its own, as matter and the bodies of this world do. Even the lowest thing in that world—the earth of the next life—is a living soul-form, higher than the sky of this world. A report says: “The ground of paradise is the Throne, and its roof is the Throne of the All-Merciful.” Water, air, fire, trees, mountains, buildings, and homes all exist there as soul-forms without matter, motion, or unrealized possibility.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00792

If even the lower, earthly things in that world exist this way, imagine how its noble, heavenly beings exist. Everything in this world has a form in the next. The difference between the heavens and earth, animals and trees, stones and water, is much greater there, because those forms are the inner realities of these things. As God says, “The next life has higher ranks and greater excellence.” Everything there is alive in its own right. We have now shown that the forms of matter, including the elements, have lasting forms in the next life. The senses can perceive them there, and they do not fade, decay, or split apart. All of them exist within the soul as if they were one power, though they have many forms and appear as many things. This is one of the wonders that only people with insight can understand. These inner forms are the hidden realities of worldly things. After their existence in this world ends, they return to those forms, are gathered there, and live through the life of the soul.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00793

The teacher of the Aristotelian philosophers says that fire has a quality like the earth's. Fire is a kind of active word within matter, as are similar things. Fire does not arise by itself without a cause, or simply through bodies rubbing together, as people think. Nor is matter itself fire in potential, or the cause that creates fire. Rather, an active word within matter produces the form of fire and all other forms. Matter receives this action. The word within it is the soul, which can shape fire and other forms. This soul is the life and active word within the fire; life and word are one. Plato therefore said that every simple body has a soul, which produces the fire we sense.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00794

If this is so, the thing that produces this fire is a kind of fiery life, a hidden fire. The fire above this fire, in the higher world, is even more truly fire. If it is a hidden fire, then it must be life. Its life is higher and nobler than the life of this fire, since this fire is only its image. So the fire in the higher world is alive, and its life gives life to this fire. The same is true of water and air there: they are alive, and their life is greater than the life they have here, because their life is what gives life to the water and air of this world.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00795

In another passage, the same philosopher says that the earth has a kind of life and an active word within it. He points to its many forms, which grow and bring forth plants, grasses, mountains, and minerals. I must say that Ibn Arabi's point is very deep, and deserves to be written in gold, not ink. Life can mean the source of awareness and action, as when we say that a living thing is aware and active. This is the life people attribute to spirits. It belongs to spirits in their own right, but to bodies only through something else. Life can also mean real, simple, all-pervading existence. Think of how people call existence itself “the life that flows through all things.” We have often said the same in this book. In this second sense, life belongs to all existing things, including bodies. How could it be otherwise, when a body exists, and existence is life in each thing according to its degree?
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00796

I say, we must understand that both direct spiritual insight and sound argument show that a body whose life belongs to its very being is not the changing physical body we see here. The bodies of this world—those in the heavens, on earth, and between them—come into being, pass away, and are renewed from moment to moment. I have explained this through reasoned proofs, scriptural evidence, and the teaching of great philosophers. How, then, could such passing bodies have life, praise, and speech simply because they are physical matter? The body whose life is truly its own is a different body, belonging to the next life. Its existence consists in being present to awareness. It does not need material support, a guiding spirit, or a soul that must first bring it from undeveloped capacity into living activity. Its existence is already life and soul. It does not require another soul to make it alive.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00797

I have often said that such a body exists as an image present to awareness. For a form of this kind, existing and being perceived are not two separate things. By contrast, the forms of physical matter do not become objects of sensation or understanding until something capable of perceiving them receives or draws them from matter. We have also shown that a form actually sensed or understood is united with the being that senses or understands it. Thus these forms belonging to awareness are alive in themselves, unlike the physical bodies that continually come into being and perish. Ibn Arabi's statement cannot, then, be accepted in its most obvious sense. The Qur'an says, “There is nothing that does not praise Him,” and other verses speak of the life and speech of all things. Those verses show that bodies are alive and give praise, whether by their own bodily existence or through the spirit or angel joined to them. They do not prove that changing matter, considered apart from any spirit or guiding form, itself speaks and praises.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00798

You have learned that every body has a form belonging to the soul and a higher source that guides it. Through these it has life and speech, not through its dark physical matter, which is mixed with absence and does not remain unchanged for even an instant. Yet there is a further subtle point that can give Ibn Arabi's words a sound meaning. Within these changing, dark bodies is another body, radiant with light and spreading through them as light spreads through crystal. Through it they receive life and come under the direction of souls and spirits. I do not mean what physicians call the animal spirit, which they describe as rising from the blood in the heart and liver and flowing through the arteries. That is a compound physical thing, found only in some bodies, and it receives life from another source. The radiant body I mean is not made up of such parts. It extends through all bodies and lives through its own existence, an existence that is itself living awareness.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00799
XIV. What “the Hour” means
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00800

God says, “They ask you about the Hour: when will it come? What have you to do with its mention? Its end rests with your Lord.” Some say it is called the Hour because souls are moving toward it, not by crossing distances in space but by passing through breaths of time, through their inner movement and natural turning toward God and His realm, as we explained in the discussion of why death is necessary. When a person dies, their Hour arrives and their Resurrection begins. This is the “small Resurrection.” We can compare it with the Great Resurrection, just as one day contains many hours, or one year many days. People with knowledge and certainty do not doubt the Hour. They know it is real.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00801

They do not wait for it as heedless people do. Those who are veiled from the truth doubt that it will happen, think it unlikely, ask when it will come, and say, “When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?” People with certainty prepare to meet it. They see it as if it were already standing over them, happening now, or close at hand. God says, “How can you know? The Hour may be near. Those who do not believe in it demand that it come sooner, but those who believe in it are wary of it and know that it is true. Those who argue about the Hour are far astray.” He also says, “The Hour is coming; there is no doubt about it, but most people do not know.” And He says, “They ask, ‘When will this promise come, if you are truthful?’ Say, ‘I have no power to help or harm myself except as God wills. Every community has its appointed time. When its time comes, they cannot delay it by a moment or bring it forward.’”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00802
XV. What it means to blow the Trumpet
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00803

God says, “The Trumpet will be blown,” and so on. The Prophet was asked about the Trumpet and said that it is a horn of light that Israfil holds to his mouth. It is described as wide at one end and narrow at the other, though people differ about which end is which. The Arabic word for the Trumpet can also mean “forms” when the vowel is changed. Al-Hasan al-Basri is reported to have read it in that way. In his great commentary on the Qur'an, al-Razi gives three meanings. First, it may mean an instrument that makes a loud sound when blown, like a horn used by a ruler to call troops. The verse would then use this instrument as an image. The report that it is a horn of light supports this reading, since light does not make a sound that the senses can hear.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00804

Second, “forms” may mean all the forms together: to blow into them would mean to breathe life into them. Al-Hasan read the word this way, as did Abu Razin, who allowed both pronunciations. This reading supports the view that the word means a collection of forms. Third, blowing the Trumpet may be a figure of speech for raising the dead and bringing them forth. Al-Razi prefers the first meaning because of the report. But the first meaning cannot be taken literally, as we have already shown, and the report itself supports that conclusion. Al-Razi also says that the phrase “then it will be blown again” shows that the verse does not mean breathing spirit into the forms, since that would not happen twice.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00805

I say that God's blowing can only mean giving life, sending forth spirit, and bringing life into being. But life in a higher world requires death in a lower one. With the first blowing, bodies die and souls live. With the second blowing, souls rise through the Real, not through their own power.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00806

All the materials of the universe, with their natural forms, can receive light from spirits. They are like charcoal that can catch fire because of the heat hidden within it. Imaginal forms are hidden within natural forms, as heat and redness are hidden in charcoal. Spirits are hidden within those imaginal forms, as flame and light are hidden in heat. With the first blowing, natural forms die away, as blackness and cold disappear when charcoal becomes red and hot. The imaginal forms are then ready to receive light from spirits, just as heated, red charcoal is ready to catch fire.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00807

When Israfil, who brings spirits into being, blows into the forms a second time, the spirits that now exist on their own light them up. God says, “Then they will rise and look around.” The Arab mystic Ibn Arabi says in The Meccan Revelations that there are two blowings: one puts out a fire, the other lights it again. Once the forms are ready, their preparation to receive spirits is like dry grass ready to catch fire. Imaginal forms are like lamps burning with the spirits within them. Israfil blows once, and that breath passes over the forms and puts them out. The next breath passes over the forms ready for the new life and lights them again. Then they rise, alive and speaking as God gives them speech. Some say, “Praise belongs to God.” Others ask, “Who has woken us from our resting place?” Others say, “Praise belongs to God, who gave us life after death. To Him we return.” Each speaks according to their state. They have forgotten their life in the intermediate world and think it was a dream, just as a person who wakes imagines their earlier life was a dream. When people die and enter the intermediate world, they wake there and think this life was a dream. In the next life, they think both this life and the intermediate life were dreams.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00808

Ibn Arabi says elsewhere that when God takes spirits from natural bodies and places them within forms gathered in the great horn of light, everything a person perceives after death in the intermediate world is perceived through the very form the person has in that horn. The two blowings are one that puts out the fire and one that lights it again. The first blowing ends the life of anyone thought to be alive, whether in heaven or on earth. God says, “The Trumpet will be blown, and all who are in the heavens and on earth will fall senseless, except those God wills.” He means those whose Great Resurrection has already happened. God also says, “Those for whom We have already promised the best reward will be kept far from it,” and goes on to say that the greatest terror will not grieve them and the angels will meet them, saying, “This is your day, the promise you were given.” Then He says, “On the day We roll up the sky as a record is rolled up.” This greatest terror is the same event as “all who are in the heavens and on earth will fall senseless.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00809

I say that those already raised are not among the people of the heavens and earth, because their true being lies beyond bodies, bodily forms, and souls. Their identities do not change with time. They are absorbed in the sea of divine oneness and the power of God's light, like the angels who are near to Him. Their identities are hidden beneath the overwhelming light of God; they do not turn back toward themselves. The second blowing brings life after death and lasting life after the end of passing life. This life is higher than the first, and its permanence is real and has no end.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00810
XVI. The small and the great Resurrection
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00811

The small Resurrection is clear: when a person dies, their Resurrection has begun. The time of the great Resurrection, however, is hidden. God has set its time, but whoever claims to know exactly when it will happen is lying. The Prophet said, “Those who set a time are liars.” Everything that happens in the great Resurrection has a counterpart in the small one.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00812

The key to understanding the Day of Resurrection and the return of all creatures is to understand the soul and its different levels. Death is like birth: use what you know about birth to understand the afterlife, and compare the great birth with the birth we know. God says, “Your creation and your rising are like the creation and rising of a single soul.” The afterlife begins when veils are lifted, coverings fall away, and realities appear. The Real is revealed in true unity, and everything appears as it truly is. If you want to understand the great Resurrection—God's revelation of Himself in true unity, all things returning to Him and losing their separate identities, even the heavens, angels, spirits, and souls—consider God's words: “All who are in the heavens and on earth will fall senseless, except those God wills.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00813

God also says, “To God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and earth,” “Everything will perish except His face,” “Everyone on earth will pass away, but the face of your Lord will remain, full of majesty and honor,” and “To God all things return.” A sound report says that God will bring every existing thing to death, even the angels, Gabriel, Israfil, Michael, and the Angel of Death, then restore them for judgment. Think about the principles we have already discussed: every lower being turns toward what is higher; each thing returns to its source; each form returns to its true reality; natural and inner change reach their ends; effects return to their causes; and the souls of the heavens join with the intellects that complete them.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00814

Anyone whose heart is lit by certainty can see the parts, beings, natures, and souls of the world changing at every moment. Everything changes; its separate identity does not last. Every existing thing returns to God, even if many cycles and ages pass first. It returns through death, disappearance, change, transformation, or the overwhelming collapse that spirits undergo. Every movement must reach an end. That end has its own end, until all ends meet in a final end with nothing beyond it. For all things, this is one divine day—or even one moment, or less—containing every time and instant in which things reach their ends. All beginnings, too, came from one beginning and one source, from which every origin branches and every cause and effect springs.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00815

The same idea becomes easier to accept when we see how all the human powers of awareness and movement, though many and different in kind, return to one simple spiritual self, are gathered into it, and then rise from it in the next life in a better and higher form. In the same way, all creatures return to God and then come forth from Him again, more complete than before. The human spirit sends the rays of its powers and senses to the body's different parts. At death, it draws their light back from those bodily channels; in the afterlife, it sends it forth again in a new way. The world is formed in the same way. All its beings—everything in the heavens, the earth, and between them—come into being, return to God as the heavens are folded up, the stars scattered, the mountains crushed, and the earth gathered in, and then begin again in a life that lasts forever.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00816

God says, “He directs the affairs from heaven to earth; then they rise back to Him on a day whose measure is a thousand years by your reckoning.” When all things return to Him, He gives them existence again, and they rise into a life that will never end. God says, “Just as We began the first creation, We will bring it back. This is a promise We will surely fulfill.” If you have not tasted this truth yourself—whether you are a scholar who has not yet reached it, someone too sure of limited reason, or someone trapped by outward forms—then trust the prophets and saints. Believe what they say about what you cannot see, as a blind person trusts the guide who leads them. Do not deny any of it. May God protect us from weak faith in the Last Day and from rejecting the great news brought by those who know. Proof, the Qur'an's signs, and the light of insight all show that the world's beings are always changing: their separate identities fade and their natures renew at every moment. God is the end of every movement and change. “To God all things return.” So glory to the One who holds the kingdom of all things in His hand; to Him you will return.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00817
XVII. Which bodies are raised in the afterlife, and which are not
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00818

As long as spirits remain spirits, they always govern bodies. There are two kinds of bodies they govern. In the first kind, the soul acts directly and inwardly, without anything in between. In the second, it acts through another body that comes first. Our outward senses cannot perceive the first kind. They perceive only bodies like the ones that carry them: outer shells, such as those of water and air, animals and plants, fine vaporous bodies, or dense flesh and plant matter. Souls govern all of these only through an intermediary. The first kind of body—the one the soul governs directly—is luminous and alive through its own life, and cannot die.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00819

It ranks above the transparent bodies we see in this world and above what is called the vital spirit. That spirit belongs to this world, though it is subtle and noble compared with other bodies. It quickly changes and fades away, so it cannot be raised into the afterlife. The bodies we are discussing are bodies of the afterlife. They rise with the souls, are joined to them, and remain as the souls remain.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00820

As for the upper intermediate realms, the highest level of this world, called the Lote Tree of the Furthest Limit, is almost pure form without matter. It is like an imaginal body, and souls act on it as they act on the forms of imagination. The levels below it are like the spirits in our brains, since they are like the imagination of the greater world. Some people of spiritual insight have said that the luminous bodies of the heavens do not have imagination as a separate power; they are imagination itself. Just as human imagination is never without images, an angel's being is never without form. The form of a heavenly sphere is to the angel what the power of imagination is to a human being. The blue sky we see is not the sky's true form, and the scattered lights we see are not its lights in the Day of Resurrection. On that day, this sky will be erased and broken apart, and its stars will be dimmed and blotted out.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00821
XVIII. The state of people of insight here
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00822

Some people see the events of the afterlife with inner sight. They witness Paradise and its people before the Hour arrives. They do not need to undergo physical death for the veils to lift from their hearts and inner vision. Their state before death is like the state of others after death. God says, “We have removed your veil, and today your sight is sharp.” This happens because their worldly state has changed into an afterlife state.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00823

When their state changes, their hearing, sight, and other senses change too. Then all the beings in heaven and earth change for them, because everything has two forms, one for this life and one for the next. Each kind of sense perceives the things that belong to its own world: the senses of this life perceive the things of this life, and the senses of the next life perceive the things of the next. God points to this change when He says, “On the day the earth is changed into another earth, and the heavens too, and all appear before God, the One, the All-Powerful.” He also says, “We have set death among you, and no one can stop Us from replacing you with others like you and bringing you into a form you do not know.” Through this change in being—whether it happens before death, at death, or after death—a person becomes ready to enter Paradise and the Abode of Peace.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00824

This also shows the difference between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell. The people of Paradise have lit hearts, open chests, purified bodies, and forms free from the impurity of natural matter. The people of Hell have not changed from their natural state. How, then, could they enter the Abode of Peace? God says, “Does every one of them hope to enter the Garden of Bliss? No. We created them from what they know”—that is, from impure seed. How could a being made from such matter be suited to the holy realm? Earthly dust is far from the Lord of all worlds.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00825

This may raise a difficult question: all people share in having been created from seed; all have natural bodies. How, then, can they become fit to enter the Abode of Peace and live near the Lord of the worlds? What does dust have in common with the Lord? God answers, “By the Lord of the Easts and the Wests, We are able to replace them with others like them and bring them into a form they do not know.” In other words, their natural state changes as they gain knowledge, faith, and good works. This change in their very being makes them ready to enter the holy realm and the world of spirits.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00826
XIX. The Straight Path
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00827

As you have learned, every being has a natural movement and an inborn tendency toward the Cause of causes. Human beings share this general movement, but they also have another movement of their own. It begins with a religious motive—a change in the soul's condition—and consists in following the way of unity and the path of those who affirm God's oneness: the prophets, the saints, and their followers. This is the path we ask God to show us when we say, “Guide us to the straight path.” It is the path described in God's words, “Say, ‘This is my way: I call to God with clear insight, I and those who follow me,’” and “You guide to a straight path, the path of God, to whom belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00828

God commands His servants to stay firm on this path and walk it without turning aside. For this reason He sent them messengers and revealed books to them. The other paths followed by created beings are not this path, which belongs to those who seek God. Each of those paths ends somewhere else, not in meeting God or drawing near to Him, and not in the Gardens or the Abode of God's good pleasure. They lead instead to the levels of Hell and its fires. The upward journey reaches God only by following the path of the fully realized human being. “Good words rise to Him, and good deeds raise them.” This is what God means when He says, “Stand firm, as you have been commanded, you and those who have turned back to God with you. Do not overstep.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00829

To turn away from this path is to fall from our original nature and follow our lower desires toward Hell. It is said to be thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword because human perfection depends on two powers. The first is the power to understand: it reaches the truth and the light of certainty by following fine lines of reasoning, so subtle that they are thinner than a hair. The second is the power to act: it brings the three powers of desire, anger, and thought into balance. This gives the soul a middle state, as far as possible, between their extremes. Every extreme is blameworthy and leads to Hell, far from God, where the wretched are turned away.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00830

You have learned that the true middle between opposing extremes is like being free of them. This freedom from the extremes is called justice. It is what saves us from Hell, and it is sharper than a sword. So the straight path has two sides: one is finer than a hair, the other sharper than a sword. Turning aside from the first means falling away from our original nature: “Those who do not believe in the Hereafter stray from the path.” Failing to keep to the second means being cut off and split apart. This is the meaning of the words, “Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?” and “They will be dragged through scalding water.” The reason is that justice is not a true perfection in itself. True perfection lies only in the light of knowledge, the strength of faith, and recognition of God. Justice is a quality of the soul that consists in a balance between its powers. It is not a positive perfection in its own right. Relying on it and being satisfied with it can keep a person attached to this world, since justice too belongs to this world. Love of this world is the root of every sin.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00831
1. A Qur'anic illumination
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00832

On the Day of Resurrection, this path will become visible to those who cross it. How clearly it appears, and how easily people make their way across it, will depend on the light of their certainty. The strength of their certainty determines how firmly and quickly they travel it. So the ranks of the blessed differ according to the light of their knowledge, certainty, and faith. We can draw near to God only through knowledge and certainty, and knowledge is light. Believers will make their way toward meeting God by the strength of their light and insight. God says, “On the Day you see believing men and women, with their light shining ahead of them and to their right, they will say, ‘Our Lord, complete our light for us…’”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00833

A report says that some people will be given a light as great as a mountain, shining ahead of them. Others will receive a smaller light. Some will have a light like a date palm in their right hand; others will have less, until the last person is given a light only as large as a toe. It will shine for a moment and then go out. When it shines in front of him, he will walk; when it goes out, he will stop.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00834

People will cross the path at different speeds, according to their light. Some will pass as quickly as the blink of an eye or a flash of light. Others will pass like a swift horse. The person whose light is no bigger than his toe will move on his face, hands, and feet, crawling and stumbling. The Fire will touch his sides. He will remain in that state until he finally gets across. This shows how much people differ in faith. One person's faith may have thousands upon thousands of times the light and strength of another's.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00835

Al-Hasan says that the path takes three thousand years to cross: a thousand years uphill, a thousand on level ground, and a thousand downhill. I think the first stage may mean the journey from creation to God, the second the journey within God, and the third the journey from God back to creation.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00836

Abu Talib al-Makki says in The Nourishment of Hearts: “It is reported that God created the Path from His mercy and brought it forth for the believers. The Path belongs to those who affirm God's oneness. The unbelievers have no passage across it, for the tyrants among them have already been seized from the gathering place by the Fire, while the rest have followed into the Fire what they used to worship instead of God.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00837

The light is divided among those who affirm God's oneness according to what they brought with them from this world. The Path grows narrower or wider according to their rank: narrow for sinners, wider for the Godfearing, and broad at its widest for the prophets and saints, like a wide carpet spread out before them. They cross at different speeds. The first pass as quickly as the blink of an eye; the last take as long as the life of the world—seven thousand years. A foot slips and burns, then the person is pulled out and healed by mercy. Then the other foot slips, just as the first has healed.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00838

“Islam came to them as mercy. When they accepted it but did not live up to it, God made a bridge for them from that mercy, so they could cross it. Whoever neglected any of the practices of Islam neglected the mercy shown to him, and his foot slipped. The Path's narrowness or breadth depends on the share of God's mercy given to each servant. The share of mercy God allotted to a person in this life determines how wide the Path will be for them there. The speed or slowness with which they cross depends on how near they are to God: the share they have of the light of nearness determines how quickly they move.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00839

“The first group crosses in the blink of an eye, like a flash of lightning. They are the prophets. The second crosses like the wind or birds; they are the truthful and the saints. The third crosses as a swift horse or a fine mount would; they are the truthful ones who struggled with themselves until they were true to God in every movement and passing thought. The fourth crosses like a rider on his mount; they are the Godfearing. The fifth runs; they are the worshippers. The sixth walks; they are those who kept their faults hidden. The seventh crawls; they are those who openly sinned while affirming God's oneness.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00840

Each group has its own light: the light of prophecy, sainthood, truthfulness, piety, worship, concealment, or the affirmation of God's oneness. Some have light that reaches as far as the eye can see; the last have light only as far as their toes. Light does not depend on how many deeds a person has done, but on how much light their deeds contain. A deed has greater light when the heart has greater light, and the heart has greater light according to its nearness to God. The nearer a person is to God, the brighter, greater, and more penetrating their light, and the more weight it carries. Many people with few deeds will reach Paradise before others whose deeds were multiplied many times over. Did you not hear the Prophet say to Mu'adh, “Be sincere, and a little action will be enough for you”? A servant can reach sincerity only through great light. That light makes their deeds pure and allows them to grow. It is said that a man from this community has surpassed people who lived a thousand years before him. A report says, “How good is the sleep and breaking of the fast of the wise! How far they surpass the night vigil and fasting of fools!” A mustard seed's worth of piety and certainty is better in God's sight than mountains of deeds done by the self-deceived. The difference in light comes from the heart's intention: some fast to obey, some to clear the heart—for hunger is a cloud that rains wisdom—some to understand the poor, and some to take on the quality of the Self-Sufficient, who does not eat. Some give to obey, some to develop generosity, some out of tenderness for the poor, and some to take on the quality of the Provider, who meets needs and provides for all creatures. The same applies to other actions.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00841

Al-Makki also says: “The straight path is the path of affirming God's oneness, the true religion followed by all the prophets, messengers, and their followers. All the noble states and stations of those traveling toward God and within God return to it. The knowledge of God's oneness is the most useful and highest of all knowledge. Indeed, it is their purest and clearest part. It is the highest aim and greatest goal. ‘Beyond Abadan there is no village.’ There is no hope of salvation except through gaining this knowledge, and no success in reaching the ranks except by harvesting its fruits. Because its rank is so high and its station so exalted, the inner sight is too weak to grasp it, minds grow ill, and eyes tire. It is a sea whose shore stops the mind; spirits and hearts cannot reach its depths.” This is the end of his words.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00842

Al-Makki is right that only the knowledge of God's oneness can bring us to nearness to God and carry us along the way. Other kinds of knowledge and good deeds matter only when they help us gain that knowledge; they are tools, not ends in themselves.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00843
2. An unveiling insight
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00844

The straight path that brings you to Paradise is the image of guidance you create for yourself through the inward work of the heart and the states of the soul while you are in the natural world. When the veil is lifted and your heart's sight is opened, you will see that the blessed human soul itself is the image of God's straight path. It has its own limits and stages. Whoever travels through them, step by step and station by station, will reach the nearness of their Lord and enter Paradise. In this world, as with other things of the afterlife, the path is hidden from our eyes and senses.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00845

When the veil is lifted at death and the covering is removed from your heart's sight, you will see it extended before you on the Day of Resurrection like a solid bridge over Hell. It begins at the gathering place and ends at one of the gates of Paradise. Those who see it will know that it is their own work and construction. Then they will understand that, in this life, it was a bridge stretched across the Hell of their own nature. That nature is like the shadow with three branches, which is “neither cool nor does it protect from the flame.” It is what leads the soul toward the blaze of its desires. The heat of that blaze will appear in the next life, though now it lies hidden within the covering of the body, like a live coal under ash. The fortunate person is the one who puts out this fire with the water of knowledge and piety.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00846

Shaykh al-Saduq says in The Beliefs: “We believe that the Path is real, that it is a bridge over Hell, and that every creature must cross it. God says, ‘There is not one of you who will not pass over it; this is a decree your Lord must fulfill.’ The Path is also a name for God's proofs. Whoever knew them in this world and obeyed them will be given a pass to cross the Path, the bridge over Hell on the Day of Resurrection.” The Prophet said to Ali, “Ali, on the Day of Resurrection, Gabriel and I will sit with you on the Path. No one will cross it unless they carry a certificate of your loyalty.” This is the end of al-Saduq's words.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00847

I find it astonishing that the Path, the one who crosses it, the distance, and the movement along it are all one thing. This is how it is on the afterlife journey taken by the human soul. The traveler toward God—the soul itself—travels within itself and crosses the stations and stages within itself by means of itself. At every step, it puts its foot on its own head, or its head on its own foot. This sounds astonishing, but it is not astonishing once you understand what is happening.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00848
XX. Spreading out the records and bringing out the books
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00849

Words and actions do not last while they remain in the changing world of material things. But when someone acts or speaks, the act or word leaves an impression in the soul, a state of the heart that lasts for a time. When actions and words are repeated, their impressions take hold in the soul and become settled traits. A passing state differs from a settled trait only in degree: as a quality grows stronger, it can become a substantial form that gives rise to that quality. A little heat in coal, for example, can intensify until it becomes a burning flame. In the same way, a state of the soul can grow into a settled trait—a lasting form in the soul that easily produces actions of its kind, without thought or effort.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00850

This is how skills and the roots of intellectual and practical learning take shape. If our souls were not first affected by actions, and if those impressions did not grow stronger day by day, no one could acquire a skill or a craft, and education and training would help no one. There would be no point in training children in useful actions before their habits became fixed in the opposite direction. It is hard to teach and discipline adults because animal qualities have become firmly rooted in their souls. Before that, their souls were open to learning and skill, like a blank page.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00851

These effects that take shape in our hearts and spirits are like writing on pages and tablets. God says, “They are the ones in whose hearts He has written faith.” In the language of religion, these hearts and spirits are called the records of deeds. Just as a page must be ready to receive writing, the writing also needs someone to produce it. Those who write this luminous record are the noble recording angels. Their own being and work are too noble for the lowliness of bodily matter; their nature rises above it.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00852

These angels are a kind of angel appointed to human actions and words. God says, “Watchers are set over you, noble writers,” and, “Two receivers sit, one on the right and one on the left. Not a word does a person utter without a watcher ready beside them.” He also says, “On the Day We call every people with their leader, those who are given their book in their right hand will read it, and they will not be wronged in the least.” And He says, “As for the one who is given his book in his right hand, he will say, ‘Here, read my book! I knew I would meet my account.’”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00853

The book of the right hand contains true knowledge and beliefs, and good character. Here “I knew” means “I was certain.” The book of the left hand contains lies, false beliefs, satanic traits, animal desires, and worldly ambitions. These burn the heart and torment the soul. A book full of lies, errors, and confused thinking deserves to burn in the Fire. God says, “As for the one who is given his book behind his back, he will call for destruction and enter a blazing Fire.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00854

A report says that when someone does a good deed, God creates an angel from it who asks forgiveness for that person until the Day of Resurrection. God says, “Those who say, ‘Our Lord is God,’ and then remain steadfast—the angels descend upon them, saying, ‘Do not fear or grieve. Rejoice in the Garden you were promised. We are your protectors in this life and in the Hereafter.’” A good deed leads to another good deed until it becomes a settled trait. The same applies in reverse to disbelief and bad beliefs. If someone forms corrupt beliefs about divine matters, clings to ignorance, and persists in disbelief, a devil descends upon them. It promises evil, deceives them through ignorance, and fills them with pride. It becomes their companion in this life and the next. God says, “Shall I tell you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every lying sinner who listens to God's signs, then persists in arrogant disbelief.” And He says, “Whoever turns away from the remembrance of the All-Merciful, We appoint a devil as his companion.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00855

A settled state of the soul that appears in a person on the Day of Resurrection is called a trait in philosophy. In religious language, a good trait is called an angel, and a bad one a devil. In reality, these names point to one thing: the settled traits of the soul become substantial forms, active in the soul, bringing it pleasure or pain. Unless these traits were stable and enduring, there would be no reason for the people of Paradise to remain forever in reward or the people of Hell forever in punishment. If reward and punishment arose only from the action or word itself, both would have disappeared. The effect would remain after its cause had vanished, which cannot be right. How could a physical act performed over a limited time lead to a reward lasting forever? Such retribution would not befit the Wise, especially in the case of punishment. God says, “I am never unjust to My servants,” and “That is because of what your hearts have earned.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00856

The people of Paradise remain in Paradise, and the people of Hell in Hell, because their intentions and settled traits endure. Yet anyone who does even an atom's weight of good or evil in this world will find its effect written in the record of their own soul or in a record above it. When the Resurrection comes and the distractions of this worldly life have ended, people will see the true face of their own being. They will look into the page of their inner life. This is what God means by, “When the records are spread open.” Someone who has ignored their own condition and failed to reckon with their good and bad deeds will say, when the veil is lifted and they come face to face with themselves, “What is this book? It leaves out nothing, small or great, but has counted it all.” They will find everything they did laid out before them, and “Your Lord wrongs no one.” God says, “On the Day every soul finds all the good it did brought before it, and all the evil it did, it will wish there were a great distance between itself and that evil.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00857

Many reports on this subject have come to us from the Prophet and the Prophet's family. One of them is this report from Qays ibn Asim. The Prophet said, “Qays, with honor comes humiliation, and with life comes death. This world has a Hereafter, and everything has a watcher and an account. Every appointed time has a written term. You must have a companion who will be buried with you while it is alive and you are dead. If it is noble, it will honor you; if it is base, it will abandon you. Then you will be raised with it, and it will be raised with you. You will be questioned only about it, so make sure it is good. If it is good, you will find comfort with it; if it is bad, you will dread only it. That companion is your own action.” Whoever reflects on this report will find in it the heart of the knowledge of the self and the afterlife, and hints at many important questions that there is no room to explain here.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00858

Among these reports is the Prophet's saying, “Paradise is barren ground, and its plants are ‘Glory be to God.’” Another says that a person is held by their deeds, and another that “the unbeliever was created from the sin of the believer.” There are many reports of this kind.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00859

Pythagoras, one of the greatest ancient sages, is reported to have said: “Your actions, words, and thoughts will be brought before you. From every movement of thought, speech, or action, a spiritual or bodily form will appear. If it comes from anger or desire, it will become a devil that torments you in this life and keeps you from meeting the light after death. But if it comes from the intellect, it will become an angel. You will enjoy its company in this life, and it will guide you in the next toward nearness to God and the Abode of His honor.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00860

What happens to each person in the afterlife is the outcome and final form of what they did in this world. God says of Noah's son—reading the word as “a deed,” rather than “an act”—“He was an unrighteous deed.” Many verses of the Qur'an show that everything a person encounters in the next life, whether in Paradise—with its maidens, palaces, fruits, and other delights—or in the Fire, with its scorpions, snakes, and other torments, is the final form of their own actions and the effects of their character. Their reward there is their very own deeds, brought to their final outcome. God says, “You will be repaid only for what you did,” and “You are repaid only for what you used to do.” He does not say “for some of what you did.” He says, “The reward of God's enemies is the Fire.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00861

To explain: the material of the people and things of the afterlife—the seeds from which its trees grow, the seed of its animals, and the underlying basis of its forms understood by the mind—is made up of inward thoughts, images formed in the soul, and ideas grasped by the intellect. The next life and everything in it are not of the same kind as this world. Things here have bodily matter that receives a form, or a soul that comes from outside, with the help of external causes and the movements and positions of the heavenly bodies. Animal bodies have a life that is added to them. But in the next life, the gardens, trees, rivers, and other things are spirits: they are images that exist on their own, and their life is their very being. Each human soul, along with its maidens, palaces, trees, and rivers, exists through one existence and lives through one life. Together they are one, yet contain many forms. When a person leaves this world, lays aside its garment, and has the veil lifted from their sight, their power to know becomes the power to see. What was hidden becomes visible. They see the outcome of their deeds and thoughts, witness the effects of their movements and actions, and read the record of their good and bad deeds.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00862

God says, “Every person has their bird fastened around their neck. On the Day of Resurrection, We will bring out for them a book they will find open: ‘Read your book! Today you are enough to call yourself to account.’” This also shows that the person in the next life is not made from natural matter, but from the images of the soul and its power to know. God says, “We will bring you into a form you do not know.” The Book of the righteous is in the highest realm, and what is there is not created from bodily matter. We know, then, that at the Resurrection a person takes form from what they know and believe. If they are filled with blameworthy desires, false hopes, and corrupt aims, they will be among the people of the Fire, burning in its torment, and their book will be in Sijjin. But if what they know is made up of holy realities and knowledge of God, His angels, His books, and His messengers, they will belong to the highest spiritual realm, the most exalted dwelling, the closest nearness, and the finest company.

XXI. The nature of reckoning and the scales
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife

You may have realized from the principles we have repeated that, on the Day of Resurrection, everyone held accountable will see the total of all their scattered actions and words, and the final account of their good and bad deeds. In their book they will find every deed, small or great. Nothing will be left out. They will find everything they did present, and their Lord will wrong no one.

An account is the gathering of separate numbers and amounts and the showing of their total. God can reveal the whole of everyone's deeds and the weight of their good and bad actions to all creatures in a single moment. He is the swiftest of those who take account. God says, “We will set up the just scales on the Day of Resurrection, and no soul will be wronged in the least. Even if a deed weighs no more than a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. We are enough to take account.” He also says, “The weighing on that Day is true. Those whose scales are heavy will be the successful; those whose scales are light are the ones who have lost themselves by wronging Our signs.”

The Qur'an uses the plural “scales” to show that there are many kinds: some measure knowledge, others measure deeds. As for the measure of knowledge, God has set down a straight balance and a clear standard from heaven. Its different parts measure the portions of spiritual provision and weigh the nourishment of the soul. By it we can tell truth from falsehood, weigh the substance of intellectual realities, and distinguish sound ideas from counterfeit ones—the pure from the mixed. God taught us how to use it and recognize its five kinds through His angels and messengers. He says, “Weigh with the straight balance.” Those who learn the measures God revealed in His Book to His Messenger are guided. Those who turn away from them and rely on guesses and opinions go astray and fall into Hell. You might ask: where are these measures of knowledge in the Qur'an? Is this not a false claim?
